messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Bartender
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Erin is a 38-year-old bartender who came to treatment months after her boyfriend was critically injured in a late-night assault outside the bar where she works. The night is fixed in her mind in flashes that still feel almost present tense: the bright spill of the neon beer sign on wet pavement, his face turning toward her when voices rose behind them, the sudden movement, blood on his shirt that looked too dark at first under the streetlight. She can describe those pieces with unnerving precision, as if they are snapshots she is forced to look at again and again. At the same time, there are stretches she cannot account for at all. She knows she screamed for help, and someone must have called 911, but the sequence between seeing him fall and finding herself in the emergency department corridor remains blank. What stands out to her most are images rather than a continuous story, and because those fragments are so sharp while the missing parts stay inaccessible, she has come to treat the gaps as evidence that she failed him in some crucial way.

In the weeks after the assault, Erin’s mind kept returning to the clearest moments, and she replayed them looking for what she should have done differently. She had urged her boyfriend to stay for one more drink after closing, and she had stepped back inside for her bag just before the confrontation began. She had come to believe the attack happened because of the way she acted, that if she had left sooner or stayed beside him continuously, none of it would have happened. The vividness of the images seemed, to her, to prove that these were the important moments she was supposed to have prevented. The blank patches did not soften that conviction; if anything, they made it worse. She was certain that if she could remember the missing minutes, they would show some additional mistake. As that belief hardened, it spread outward into a broader mistrust. She found herself thinking that people were not what they seemed, that danger could surface from ordinary faces without warning, and that relying on anyone else was how people got hurt.

Those beliefs shaped how she tried to get through each day. Erin began avoiding news reports about assaults, hospital stories, or any segment about random violence, switching channels or leaving the room before details could begin. She told herself there was no point in taking in more examples of what people were capable of. She also worked hard to keep a lid on any feeling that threatened to break through. During her shifts, if a customer’s raised voice or the scrape of shoes outside the front door brought up one of those frozen images, she would straighten glasses, focus on receipts, and clamp down on any sign of panic or grief. She has not sought medical or psychological help until now, in part because she does not believe other people can really be counted on, and in part because asking for help feels to her like handing control to someone who might fail her the way she believes she failed her boyfriend.

The bar itself has become one of the places where the problem is most visible. Near closing time, when the lighting changes and patrons drift out in uneven clusters, she is pulled back by specific visual fragments from that night. A man in a dark jacket pausing under the beer sign, a smear of red cocktail on the counter, an ambulance siren passing outside can bring the memory up in pictures so immediate that for a moment she feels pinned inside them. Those moments make her even more guarded. She watches customers closely, assumes friendliness can turn without warning, and avoids leaning on the bouncer or her coworkers even when they offer to walk her to her car. The memories leave her feeling that only constant self-control keeps things from getting worse, so she doubles down on staying composed and refusing help.

Over time, those strategies have fed back into the way she sees herself and other people. Because she avoids reminders in the news and has stayed away from medical and psychological settings, nothing has challenged her conviction that the world is fundamentally deceptive and that she alone is responsible for preventing disaster. Because she spends so much effort suppressing emotion, she experiences any crack in that control as further proof that she is not handling this well enough. She has become more distant with her boyfriend since his physical recovery, not because she cares less, but because she cannot bear to hear his version of the night or risk learning that he blames her too. What finally brought her in was a recent shift when a customer collapsed after being cut on broken glass and, before anyone even knew the injury was minor, Erin felt the old images slam back so clearly that she had to retreat to the stockroom. She is seeking help now because she is frightened that her life has narrowed to vigilance, silence, and self-blame, and because some part of her still hopes there may be a way to remember what happened without feeling condemned by it.
